title: The view from the top
hook: look back at five years: the stories, the practices, the texts, the questions, your own rule
tomorrow: why do the mountaintop stories end on the way down?

segments.voice: Yesterday, we climbed together: Marcus's book of names, and the names on this path. Now, the top, and a poet with a book in his pocket.

At the top of anything, a trail, a graduation, a finished project, the phone comes out for the view. Petrarch, the Italian poet, climbed Mont Ventoux with his brother and wrote a letter about it. At the summit he took in the clouds below, the far mountains, the distant sea. Then he opened the small copy of Augustine's Confessions he carried, at random. On the page: people go out to admire the heights of mountains, the waves of the sea, the courses of the stars, "and pass themselves by."
screen: `THE PHONE COMES OUT.` → `PETRARCH ON MONT VENTOUX.` → `AND PASS THEMSELVES BY.`

segments.voice: Petrarch wrote that he was stunned, and angry with himself for admiring earthly things. He closed the book and turned his eyes inward, and he says he hardly spoke on the way down. That's Augustine's teaching: God and truth are found by turning inward, not only by looking out. Augustine wrote that God was within him while he went searching outside. But notice what Petrarch did before he opened the book. At the top, his letter says, he also looked back over his own years: how he had changed, and what he still struggled with. That's the view from the top, both directions. Outward: look how far the trail came, every switchback visible from here. Inward: the slower view, how far you came. All the days on this path: stories told properly, practices, old texts, hard questions, and a rule of your own. Augustine's line is a warning not to skip that second view. At the top, don't pass yourself by.
screen: `HE TURNED HIS EYES INWARD.` · `GOD WITHIN, WHILE HE SEARCHED OUTSIDE.` · `OUTWARD: HOW FAR THE TRAIL CAME.` · `INWARD: HOW FAR YOU CAME.` · then, large: `LOOK HOW FAR.`

segments.voice: Stand at a window, or anywhere you can see a little distance. Look out first, as far as you can see, then let your eyes soften and take the inward view: one way you're different from when you began.
The view from the top: Petrarch's summit, and Augustine's warning not to pass yourself by on the way.
screen: `THE VIEW FROM THE TOP — today's word`.

segments.voice: The line to keep: look how far, out at the trail and in at the one who walked it. One day to the summit.

screen: `DAY 1790 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 14 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DO MOUNTAINTOP STORIES END ON THE WAY DOWN?`

howItsDone: Augustine's Confessions are read for their turn inward toward God; Petrarch's letter about Mont Ventoux is read as a story of looking out and then within. People on this path look back at how far they've come, inside as well as out.

Petrarch.meaning: an Italian poet and scholar who wrote about his climb

Mont Ventoux.meaning: a tall mountain in southern France

Augustine.meaning: a North African bishop whose Confessions tell his search for God

Confessions.meaning: Augustine's own story of his life, addressed to God
